citations.context: And as the angel is getting ready to kill all of Jerusalem, is what it says. God has to stay the hand of the angel. He relents from the calamity that he chose to cause, changing his mind. In Jonah 3:10, we see him doing this with the people in Nineveh. And in Amos 7 3, so the Lord relented, this will not happen, says the Lord. That's God changing his mind. It's not the only time. We could point to just abstract, obvious things where God has changed his mind. For example, God says slavery is bad when he wants to rescue his people from being enslaved.

citations.context: Now, this third one that I want to highlight is can God change his mind? According to Numbers chapter 23, verse 19, God is not a man that he should lie or change his mind. But according to Jonah chapter 3, verse 10, God changed his mind and did not destroy Nineveh. Now, Exodus chapter 32, verse 14 says, So the Lord changed his mind. Now this is a clear contradiction, and the question is, is this immutable or reactive?

citations.context: Now again, Numbers chapter 23 says, God is not a man that he should lie, nor a son of man that he should change his mind. There is a clear claim there that God does not change his mind. And then in Jonah chapter 3, verse 10, it says, when God saw what they did, he changed his mind about the calamity he had said he would bring upon them, and he did not do it. The clear claim here is that God changed his mind based on human behavior. And then even when we look back at Exodus 32, so the Lord changed his mind about the disaster he planned to bring on his people.
